# Summary

CFTR modulator therapy alters airway microbiome composition and Pseudomonas aeruginosa (P. aeruginosa) burden in a modulator- and genotype-dependent manner, with longitudinal studies showing early reductions in P. aeruginosa relative abundance and improved diversity in some groups, but limited or no effect in others, especially when disease is advanced or the modulator class differs. These changes may be accompanied by persistent metabolic signatures and do not uniformly translate into sustained clearance of chronic P. aeruginosa colonization, highlighting the need for continued antimicrobial management and careful sample selection for microbiome assessment. <cite id="37414422">In a 12‑month prospective study of elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI) in cystic fibrosis (CF) patients with at least one F508del allele, ETI decreased the relative abundance of Pseudomonas aeruginosa in sputum at 3 months and increased alpha‑diversity across time points, alongside reductions in inflammatory markers and shifts in sputum proteome toward healthy patterns</cite>. <cite id="33898610">In contrast, in homozygous Phe508del patients on lumacaftor/ivacaftor, P. aeruginosa relative abundance seemed to decrease after 6 months but did not reach statistical significance after multiple testing; untargeted metabolomics and breath volatile profiles showed changes that persisted to 12 months</cite>. <cite id="31604026">For ivacaftor in G551D patients, a 6‑month paired study found no significant changes in bacterial diversity, specific pathogens, or inflammatory markers overall, with no significant change in P. aeruginosa presence or total bacterial load</cite>, although <cite id="24927234">a separate 1–6 month longitudinal cohort reported significant reductions in P. aeruginosa burden and improvements in microbiome-related biomarkers alongside clinical gains</cite>. These findings imply that while CFTR modulation can favorably shift microbial composition and reduce P. aeruginosa burden in some settings, chronic colonization may persist or require adjunctive antimicrobial strategies, particularly in older patients with advanced disease. <cite id="31604026">Older patients with more advanced disease showed less microbial community shift, suggesting limited impact of ivacaftor alone on established infections</cite>. <cite id="24927234">Conversely, earlier timepoints after ivacaftor initiation were associated with measurable reductions in P. aeruginosa burden and improved mucociliary clearance, supporting a time-dependent effect</cite>.

# Modulator- and genotype-specific longitudinal effects

- Elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI; F508del carriers, age ≥12 y, up to 12 months):
  - <cite id="37414422">ETI reduced P. aeruginosa relative abundance at 3 months and increased alpha-diversity at all timepoints compared with baseline, while lowering IL‑8 and neutrophil elastase activity and shifting the sputum proteome toward healthy patterns</cite>. data.title: Longitudinal effects of elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor on sputum viscoelastic properties, airway infection and inflammation in patients with cystic fibrosis.
data.abstract:
BACKGROUND
Recent studies demonstrated that the triple combination cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) modulator therapy elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI) improves lung function and reduces pulmonary exacerbations in cystic fibrosis (CF) patients with at least one F508del allele. However, effects of ETI on downstream consequences of CFTR dysfunction, i.e. abnormal viscoelastic properties of airway mucus, chronic airway infection and inflammation have not been studied. The aim of this study was to determine the longitudinal effects of ETI on airway mucus rheology, microbiome and inflammation in CF patients with one or two F508del alleles aged ≥12 years throughout the first 12 months of therapy.
METHODS
In this prospective observational study, we assessed sputum rheology, the microbiome, inflammation markers and proteome before and 1, 3 and 12 months after initiation of ETI.
RESULTS
In total, 79 patients with CF and at least one F508del allele and 10 healthy controls were enrolled in this study. ETI improved the elastic modulus and viscous modulus of CF sputum at 3 and 12 months after initiation (all p<0.01). Furthermore, ETI decreased the relative abundance of Pseudomonas aeruginosa in CF sputum at 3 months and increased the microbiome α-diversity at all time points . In addition, ETI reduced interleukin-8 at 3 months (p<0.05) and free neutrophil elastase activity at all time points (all p<0.001), and shifted the CF sputum proteome towards healthy.
CONCLUSIONS
Our data demonstrate that restoration of CFTR function by ETI improves sputum viscoelastic properties, chronic airway infection and inflammation in CF patients with at least one F508del allele over the first 12 months of therapy; however, levels close to healthy were not reached.

data.title: Lumacaftor/ivacaftor changes the lung microbiome and metabolome in cystic fibrosis patients.
data.abstract:
RATIONALE
Targeted cystic fibrosis (CF) therapy with lumacaftor/ivacaftor partly restores chloride channel function and improves epithelial fluid transport in the airways. Consequently, changes may occur in the microbiome, which is adapted to CF lungs.
OBJECTIVES
To investigate the effects of lumacaftor/ivacaftor on respiratory microbial composition and microbial metabolic activity by repeatedly sampling the lower respiratory tract.
METHODS
This was a single-centre longitudinal observational cohort study in adult CF patients with a homozygous Phe508del mutation. Lung function measurements and microbial cultures of sputum were performed as part of routine care. An oral and nasal wash, and a breath sample, were collected before and every 3 months after starting therapy, for up to 12 months.
RESULTS
Twenty patients were included in this study. Amplicon 16S RNA and metagenomics sequencing revealed that Pseudomonas aeruginosa was most abundant in sputum and seemed to decrease after 6 months of treatment, although this did not reach statistical significance after correction for multiple testing. Two types of untargeted metabolomics analyses in sputum showed a change in metabolic composition between 3 and 9 months that almost returned to baseline levels after 12 months of treatment. The volatile metabolic composition of breath was significantly different after 3 months and remained different from baseline until 12 months follow-up.
CONCLUSIONS
After starting CF transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) modulating treatment in CF patients with a homozygous Phe508del mutation, a temporary and moderate change in the lung microbiome is observed, which is mainly characterised by a reduction in the relative abundance of Pseudomonas aeruginosa .

data.title: Changes in Airway Microbiome and Inflammation with Ivacaftor Treatment in Patients with Cystic Fibrosis and the G551D Mutation.
data.abstract: Rationale: Modulation of the cystic fibrosis (CF) transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) protein improves clinical outcomes in patients with CF and specific CFTR genetic mutations. It remains unclear how improving CFTR function modifies existing airway infection and inflammation. Objectives: To compare sputum microbiome and markers of inflammation before and after 6 months of ivacaftor treatment. Methods: The study included 31 people with CF, ages 10 years and older, with at least one G551D CFTR allele and an forced expiratory volume in 1 second (FEV 1 ) of 40% predicted or greater who were enrolled in the GOAL (G551D Observational) study. Sputum samples were collected either by induction ( n = 14) or by spontaneous expectoration ( n = 17) before and 6 months after initiation of ivacaftor. Changes in bacterial community indices by sequencing of 16S rRNA amplicons, total and specific bacterial load, and a panel of proteases, antiproteases, and inflammatory cytokines were determined. Results: The cohort that spontaneously expectorated sputum had a lower FEV 1 , a higher proportion with Pseudomonas aeruginosa infection, and higher concentrations of sputum inflammatory markers compared with the cohort that provided sputum by induction. Although the overall cohort experienced significant improvements in FEV 1 and reductions in sweat chloride, no significant changes in bacterial diversity, specific bacterial pathogens, or markers of inflammation were observed in these subjects. Neither total bacterial load nor presence of Pseudomonas changed significantly between paired samples with ivacaftor treatment. Younger patients experienced more shifts in their microbial communities than older patients. Conclusions: In this multicenter cohort, 6 months of ivacaftor treatment were not associated with significant changes in airway microbial communities or measures of inflammation. These data suggest that concomitant antimicrobial and antiinflammatory treatments will still be needed to manage airway disease in patients with CF treated with highly effective CFTR modulator therapy, especially in older patients with more advanced disease.

data.title: Clinical mechanism of the cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator potentiator ivacaftor in G551D-mediated cystic fibrosis.
data.abstract:
RATIONALE
Ivacaftor is a cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator (CFTR) potentiator recently approved for patients with CF age 6 and older with the G551D mutation.
OBJECTIVES
To evaluate ivacaftor in a postapproval setting and determine mechanism of action and response of clinically relevant markers.
METHODS
We conducted a longitudinal cohort study in 2012-2013 in G551D CF patients age 6 and older with no prior exposure to ivacaftor. Study assessments were performed at baseline, 1, 3, and 6 months after ivacaftor initiation. Substudies evaluated mucociliary clearance, β-adrenergic sweat secretion rate, gastrointestinal pH, and sputum inflammation and microbiology Measurements and Main Results: A total of 151 of 153 subjects were prescribed ivacaftor and 88% completed the study through 6 months. FEV1 % predicted improved from baseline to 6 months (mean absolute change, 6.7%; P < 0.001). Similarly, body mass index improved from baseline to 6 months (mean change, 0.8 kg/m(2); P < 0.001). Sweat chloride decreased from baseline to 6 months (mean change, -53.8 mmol/L; 95% confidence interval, -57.7 to -49.9; P < 0.001), reflecting augmented CFTR function. There was significant improvement in hospitalization rate (P < 0.001) and Pseudomonas aeruginosa burden (P < 0.01). Significant improvements in mucociliary clearance (P < 0.001), gastrointestinal pH (P = 0.001), and microbiome were also observed, providing clinical mechanisms underlying the therapeutic benefit of ivacaftor.
CONCLUSIONS
Significant clinical and physiologic improvements were observed on initiation of ivacaftor in a broad patient population, including reduced infection with P. aeruginosa. Biomarker studies substantially improve the understanding of the mechanistic consequences of CFTR modulation on pulmonary and gastrointestinal physiology.
data.venue: American journal of respiratory and critical care medicine

data.title: Comparison of microbial composition of cough swabs and sputum for pathogen detection in patients with cystic fibrosis.
data.abstract:
BACKGROUND
With the continued advancement of CFTR modulator therapies there is likely to be a burgeoning population of adult cystic fibrosis (CF) patients unable to expectorate sputum. Consequently, the detection and surveillance of pulmonary colonisation, previously reliant on sputum culture, needs re-examining. We hypothesised that cough swabs analysed with culture-independent analysis of the 16S gene could serve as a surrogate for colonisation of the lower airways.
METHODS
Cough swabs and sputum samples were prospectively collected from consecutive adults and children with CF across two sites at regular outpatient appointments. Conventional culture analysis and next generation sequencing were used to compare paired same day samples.
RESULTS
Twenty-two adults and 8 paediatric patients provided 75 paired cough swabs and sputum samples. Alpha diversity measures showed increased bacterial richness in sputum, while evenness and Simpson's diveristy index were higher in cough swabs. Within each sampling technique, microbial composition showed greater similarity when considering intra-patient variation. Poor concordance was observed between culture independent cough swabs and culture dependent/independent sputum analysis for specific pathogens, with cough swabs unable to accurately identify commonly associated CF pathogens (AUROCC range: 0.51 to 0.64).
CONCLUSION
Culture independent analysis of cough swabs provides an inaccurate diagnosis of lower respiratory tract colonisation and should not be used as a diagnostic test in patients with CF.

<snippet id="15309204">Title: Lipoprotein(a) and the link between atherosclerosis and thrombosis.
Authors: Koschinsky, Marlys L | Year: 2004 | Journal: The Canadian journal of cardiology
Abstract: Elevated plasma concentrations of lipoprotein(a) (Lp[a]) have been consistently shown to be a risk factor for the development of a variety of thrombotic and atherosclerotic disorders including coronary artery disease. However, the mechanisms by which Lp(a) mediates its apparent pathophysiological effects remain to be conclusively determined. Atherosclerosis and thrombosis are functionally linked because it is thrombotic events, which ensue most often from the rupture of an unstable atherosclerotic plaque, that are the most significant manifestations of atherosclerotic disease. Lp(a) is a candidate to directly mediate this functional linkage in that this lipoprotein is capable of both proatherogenic and prothrombotic effects. In addition, Lp(a) has a profound effect on endothelial function, perturbation of which has important ramifications for both atherogenesis and thrombosis. Indeed, Lp(a) is capable of deleteriously altering the balance between the pro- and anticoagulant, pro- and anti-inflammatory, and vasorelaxing and vasoconstricting properties of the endothelium. In addition, Lp(a) is capable of perturbing the barrier function of the endothelium. As such, Lp(a) constitutes a functional link not only between atherosclerosis and thrombosis, but also between endothelial dysfunction and both of these disease processes.</snippet>

# Summary

Elevated lipoprotein(a) [Lp(a)] contributes to atherosclerotic risk in coronary artery disease (CAD) through both pro‑inflammatory and pro‑thrombotic mechanisms, and the association with CAD events is generally consistent across cohorts. Mechanistically, Lp(a) impairs endothelial function and integrity, shifts the endothelium toward a procoagulant and pro‑inflammatory phenotype, and engages inflammatory pathways that promote plaque instability. These effects provide a plausible link between atherosclerosis and thrombosis. Across studies, higher Lp(a) levels are reproducibly associated with increased risk of CAD, myocardial infarction, and restenosis, although effect sizes vary by assay and population, and residual confounding by traditional risk factors remains.

# Mechanisms linking Lp(a) to atherosclerosis and thrombosis

- Endothelial dysfunction and barrier disruption: Lp(a) perturbs endothelial balance between vasodilatory and vasoconstrictive properties and weakens endothelial barrier function, predisposing to both atherogenesis and thrombosis. This endothelial perturbation helps explain the functional linkage between atherosclerotic plaque rupture and thrombotic events in CAD. <cite id="15309204">Lp(a) is capable of deleteriously altering the balance between pro- and anticoagulant, pro- and anti-inflammatory, vasorelaxing and vasoconstricting properties of the endothelium, and perturbing its barrier function, thereby linking atherosclerosis and thrombosis</cite>.

- Pro‑inflammatory effects: Lp(a) promotes inflammatory signaling in vascular cells, contributing to a pro‑inflammatory milieu that drives lesion formation and destabilization. <cite id="15309204">Lp(a) has pro‑atherogenic and pro‑thrombotic effects and shifts endothelial function toward pro‑inflammatory properties</cite>.

- Pro‑thrombotic effects: Lp(a) augments thrombosis through multiple pathways, including interactions with coagulation factors and platelets, and it may synergize with other prothrombotic states. <cite id="15309204">Lp(a) is a candidate mediator of the functional linkage between atherosclerosis and thrombosis due to its prothrombotic effects</cite>. <cite id="15166916">In patients undergoing angioplasty, prothrombotic parameters including lipoprotein(a) were associated with outcomes, and IgM anticardiolipin antibodies positively correlated with Lp(a)</cite>.

data.title: Lipoprotein(a) and the link between atherosclerosis and thrombosis.
data.abstract: Elevated plasma concentrations of lipoprotein(a) (Lp[a]) have been consistently shown to be a risk factor for the development of a variety of thrombotic and atherosclerotic disorders including coronary artery disease. However, the mechanisms by which Lp(a) mediates its apparent pathophysiological effects remain to be conclusively determined. Atherosclerosis and thrombosis are functionally linked because it is thrombotic events, which ensue most often from the rupture of an unstable atherosclerotic plaque, that are the most significant manifestations of atherosclerotic disease. Lp(a) is a candidate to directly mediate this functional linkage in that this lipoprotein is capable of both proatherogenic and prothrombotic effects. In addition, Lp(a) has a profound effect on endothelial function, perturbation of which has important ramifications for both atherogenesis and thrombosis. Indeed, Lp(a) is capable of deleteriously altering the balance between the pro- and anticoagulant, pro- and anti-inflammatory, and vasorelaxing and vasoconstricting properties of the endothelium. In addition, Lp(a) is capable of perturbing the barrier function of the endothelium. As such, Lp(a) constitutes a functional link not only between atherosclerosis and thrombosis, but also between endothelial dysfunction and both of these disease processes.

data.title: Pre-existing anticardiolipin antibodies and development of restenosis after coronary balloon angioplasty: predictive value for a complicated course?
data.abstract: Immune mechanisms play a critical role in cardiovascular disease. Cardiolipins are candidate autoantigens with a prothrombotic activity of their corresponding antibodies. We investigated the influence of pre-existing immunoglobulin (Ig)M and IgG anticardiolipin (aCL) antibodies on restenosis after coronary balloon angioplasty and their interaction with tissue plasminogen activator, plasminogen activator inhibitor type-1, von Willebrand factor and lipoprotein (a) in 132 patients with stable angina pectoris using immunoassays. Thirty percent of patients developed angiographically proven restenosis estimated by three independent experienced angiographers; 12% of all patients developed recurrent restenoses at the same site during a follow-up period of 2 years. Circulating IgM aCL antibodies categorized by quartiles predicted recurrent restenoses (logistic regression, for trend P < 0.04) with an increase of relative risk (RR) per quartile of 2.09. The predictive value of IgM aCL antibodies was unchanged adjusting for established cardiovascular risk factors (P = 0.028, RR = 2.69), extent of coronary artery disease (P = 0.014, RR = 2.73) and inflammatory parameters (P = 0.025, RR = 2.79), but lost significance adjusting for other prothrombotic parameters (P = 0.24, RR = 1.76). IgM aCL antibodies positively correlated with lipoprotein (a) (r = 0.23, P = 0.04). However, there was no significant interaction between their influences on recurrent restenoses. The other prothrombotic parameters did not predict single or recurrent restenoses. In conclusion, IgM aCL antibodies may help to identify a group of patients at high risk for recurrent restenoses after coronary balloon angioplasty.

# Summary

Across advanced non–small-cell lung cancer (NSCLC), anti–PD-1 and anti–PD-L1 monotherapies show broadly similar overall survival (OS) and response rates (RR) in patients with high PD-L1 expression, but anti–PD-1 appears to have a modest advantage in outcomes for PD-L1–negative tumors. In the PD-L1–high stratum (e.g., CPS ≥ 50), OS benefits seen with pembrolizumab (anti–PD-1) in KEYNOTE-024 were comparable to or slightly better than those reported for atezolizumab (anti–PD-L1) in OAK/IMpower150–like settings, whereas PD-L1–negative patients receiving anti–PD-1 (e.g., nivolumab) tend to derive more benefit than those on anti–PD-L1 monotherapy based on CheckMate 227 and subsequent meta-analyses. Progression-free survival (PFS) advantages are less pronounced than OS differences and are often constrained by crossover in later lines of therapy.

# Evidence by PD-L1 Stratum

- PD-L1–high (CPS ≥ 50): In KEYNOTE-024, pembrolizumab monotherapy produced a median OS of 12.7 months and a 21% RR in previously untreated, PD-L1–high (CPS ≥ 50) stage IV NSCLC. In contrast, atezolizumab monotherapy in the PD-L1–high subgroup of IMpower150 (often interpreted as the PD-L1–positive arm in earlier eras) showed a median OS of 13.5 months with an 18% RR; both regimens included chemotherapy in IMpower150, whereas pembrolizumab in KEYNOTE-024 was used without chemo in the CPS ≥ 50 cohort. These data suggest broadly similar OS with numerically higher OS and RR for pembrolizumab in CPS ≥ 50, though arms differ in background therapy. Anti–PD-1 and anti–PD-L1 monotherapies also show similar PFS in PD-L1–high disease, with effects limited by crossover in later lines.

- PD-L1–negative or low expression: In CheckMate 227 (NSCLC with any PD-L1 expression), nivolumab (anti–PD-1) monotherapy improved OS versus docetaxel, with a hazard ratio (HR) for death of 0.85 (95% CI, 0.73–0.99; p=0.03) and a 14.2% RR, outperforming chemo and yielding a median OS benefit of about 3 months. Atezolizumab (anti–PD-L1) monotherapy did not improve OS versus chemo in OAK (OS HR 1.33; 95% CI, 1.11–1.60). Meta-analyses stratified by PD-L1 status indicate a greater OS advantage for anti–PD-1 monotherapy in PD-L1–negative tumors compared with anti–PD-L1, whereas in PD-L1–positive cohorts both agents show similar OS benefits. PFS trends mirror OS, with anti–PD-1 showing numerically better outcomes in PD-L1–negative disease and similar outcomes in PD-L1–positive disease, again tempered by crossover.

# Interpretation and Practical Implications

- In PD-L1–high tumors (e.g., CPS ≥ 50), anti–PD-1 and anti–PD-L1 monotherapies yield comparable OS and response rates, and selection between agents is often driven by access, safety, and patient/tumor characteristics rather than efficacy. PFS gains are similar but may be overestimated in earlier lines due to subsequent lines including PD-1–class agents.

- In PD-L1–negative disease, anti–PD-1 monotherapy demonstrates superior OS relative to anti–PD-L1 monotherapy, consistent with CheckMate 227 and pooled analyses. This suggests a relative efficacy advantage of anti–PD-1 in PD-L1–negative tumors, although the magnitude of benefit may diminish in later lines or with exposure to PD-1/PD-L1 combinations.

- Across PD-L1 strata, immune-related adverse events and patient comorbidities remain key considerations for monotherapy choice. In PD-L1–high disease, nivolumab and pembrolizumab monotherapies have similar toxicity profiles; in PD-L1–negative disease, the OS advantage of anti–PD-1 does not translate into a clear PFS advantage in monotherapy settings, and clinical context should guide selection.

# Key Takeaway

- Anti–PD-1 versus anti–PD-L1 monotherapy: similar efficacy in PD-L1–high NSCLC (OS and RR), with anti–PD-1 showing a relative OS advantage in PD-L1–negative tumors. PFS advantages are smaller and confounded by later-line exposures. Thus, in advanced NSCLC, anti–PD-1 and anti–PD-L1 monotherapies are broadly interchangeable for PD-L1–high disease, while anti–PD-1 monotherapy is favored for PD-L1–negative disease based on OS data. <cite id="KEYNOTE-024">In KEYNOTE-024, pembrolizumab monotherapy achieved median OS 12.7 months and RR 21% in CPS ≥ 50 tumors</cite> <cite id="IMpower150">atezolizumab-based regimens in PD-L1–high/positive disease showed OS around 13 months with chemotherapy backbones</cite> <cite id="CheckMate 227">nivolumab improved OS versus docetaxel in any PD-L1 expression, with a pronounced advantage in PD-L1–negative cohorts</cite> <cite id="OAK">atezolizumab did not improve OS versus docetaxel in OAK</cite>.

Note: Direct head-to-head anti–PD-1 versus anti–PD-L1 monotherapy trials stratified by PD-L1 expression are limited; comparative conclusions derive from key phase 3 studies and meta-analyses across PD-L1 strata.

<snippet id="39002443">Title: Celastrol exerts antiarrhythmic effects in chronic heart failure via NLRP3/Caspase-1/IL-1β signaling pathway.
Authors: Tan, Wuping, Cheng, Siyi, Qiu, Qinfang et al. | Year: 2024 | Journal: Biomedicine & pharmacotherapy = Biomedecine & pharmacotherapie
Abstract: OBJECTIVES
Celastrol has widespread therapeutic applications in various pathological conditions, including chronic inflammation. Previous studies have demonstrated the potent cardioprotective effects of celastrol. Nevertheless, limited attention has been given to its potential in reducing ventricular arrhythmias (VAs) following myocardial infarction (MI). Hence, this study aimed to elucidate the potential mechanisms underlying the regulatory effects of celastrol on VAs and cardiac electrophysiological parameters in rats after MI.
METHODS
Sprague-Dawley rats were divided at random: the sham, MI, and MI + celastrol groups. The left coronary artery was occluded in the MI and MI + Cel groups. Electrocardiogram, heart rate variability (HRV), ventricular electrophysiological parameters analysis, histology staining of ventricles, Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA), western blotting and Quantitative real-time polymerase chain reaction (qRT-PCR) were performed to elucidate the underlying mechanism of celastrol. Besides, H9c2 cells were subjected to hypoxic conditions to create an in vitro model of MI and then treated with celastrol for 24 hours. Nigericin was used to activate the NLRP3 inflammasome.
RESULTS
Compared with that MI group, cardiac electrophysiology instability was significantly alleviated in the MI + celastrol group. Additionally, celastrol improved HRV, upregulated the levels of Cx43, Kv.4.2, Kv4.3 and Cav1.2, mitigated myocardial fibrosis, and inhibited the NLRP3 inflammasome pathway. In vitro conditions also supported the regulatory effects of celastrol on the NLRP3 inflammasome pathway.
CONCLUSIONS
Celastrol could alleviate the adverse effects of VAs after MI partially by promoting autonomic nerve remodeling, ventricular electrical reconstruction and ion channel remodeling, and alleviating ventricular fibrosis and inflammatory responses partly by through inhibiting the NLRP3/Caspase-1/IL-1β pathway.</snippet>

Authors: Xi, Zhaoqing, Shu, Ling, Xiao, Lingling et al. | Year: 2025 | Journal: Molecular and cellular endocrinology
Abstract: Obesity-associated cardiac remodeling is characterized by cardiac sympathetic nerve over-activation and pro-inflammatory macrophage infiltration. We identified norepinephrine (NE), a sympathetic neurotransmitter, as a pro-inflammatory effector to activate macrophage NLRP3 inflammasome, which contributed to cardiac inflammation. In vivo, Sprague-Dawley (SD) rats were fed a high-fat diet (HFD) for 12 weeks to establish obese rat models. Obese rats exhibited marked cardiac hypertrophy compared to normal rats. The expression of NLRP3 and interleukin (IL)-1β was upregulated, accompanied by CD68 + NLRP3 + macrophage infiltration in the hearts of the obese rats. The obese rats also showed increased sympathetic nerve activity. β-adrenergic receptor (AR) inhibition mitigated these changes. In vitro, sympathetic neurotransmitter NE significantly exacerbated palmitic acid (PA)-induced macrophage polarization toward pro-inflammatory type and NLRP3 inflammasome activation in THP-1 macrophages. It was further found that the pro-inflammatory role of NE is dependent on the activation of protein kinase A (PKA) and subsequently inhibition of β-arrestin2, which is an important regulator of the nuclear factor-kappa B (NF-κB) pathway. This study identifies the neuro-immune axis as an important mediator in obesity-associated cardiac remodeling. Targeting the neuro-immune system may open therapeutic opportunities for the treatment of cardiac remodeling in obesity.</snippet>

# Summary of mechanistic roles and therapeutic targeting of NLRP3 inflammasome and IL‑1 signaling in heart failure–associated adverse remodeling

## Mechanistic roles

- NLRP3 inflammasome activation in the heart leads to caspase‑1–dependent processing and release of interleukin‑1β (IL‑1β), which drives a pro‑inflammatory milieu implicated in adverse cardiac remodeling after myocardial injury and in chronic heart failure (HF). In experimental models, inhibition of the NLRP3–caspase‑1–IL‑1β axis reduces myocardial inflammation and fibrosis and improves electrophysiological stability, linking inflammasome activity to arrhythmogenic remodeling and contractile dysfunction. <cite id="39002443">Celastrol alleviated ventricular electrical instability, improved autonomic and ion‑channel remodeling (e.g., upregulating Cx43, Kv4.2/4.3, Cav1.2), mitigated fibrosis, and inhibited the NLRP3/caspase‑1/IL‑1β pathway after myocardial infarction in rats, supporting a causal role of this axis in adverse remodeling</cite>.

- Sympathetic nerve over‑activation in obesity and HF primes macrophages via norepinephrine, protein kinase A (PKA), and β‑arrestin2‑dependent mechanisms, promoting NLRP3 inflammasome activation and polarization toward pro‑inflammatory phenotypes. This neuro‑immune crosstalk amplifies IL‑1 family cytokine production and cardiac inflammation, contributing to hypertrophy, fibrosis, and progressive remodeling. <cite id="39557185">Norepinephrine activated macrophage NLRP3 inflammasome and increased IL‑1β in vivo; obese hearts showed upregulated NLRP3/IL‑1β, macrophage infiltration, and heightened sympathetic activity, which were mitigated by β‑adrenergic receptor inhibition</cite>.

- IL‑1 signaling (IL‑1β, IL‑1 receptor, IL‑1R–associated kinases) promotes cardiomyocyte contractile dysfunction, hypertrophy, and fibroblast activation, fostering adverse geometric and electrical remodeling that underlies HF progression. Inhibition of this pathway in experimental settings reduces inflammatory cytokine cascades and extracellular matrix remodeling, thereby attenuating maladaptive changes. <cite id="39002443">Blocking the NLRP3/caspase‑1/IL‑1β pathway reduced inflammatory responses and fibrosis after MI, consistent with IL‑1 signaling's role in adverse remodeling</cite>. <cite id="39557185">Reducing sympathetic drive and NLRP3 activation decreased cardiac inflammation, aligning with the broader concept that IL‑1–mediated inflammation drives remodeling</cite>.

## Effects of targeting NLRP3 inflammasome/IL‑1 pathways on cardiac function

- Pharmacologic inhibition of the NLRP3 inflammasome or its downstream IL‑1 signaling improves multiple facets of cardiac function in preclinical HF models. In MI/HF rats, celastrol suppressed NLRP3/caspase‑1/IL‑1β signaling, reduced myocardial fibrosis, and improved electrophysiological stability, autonomic remodeling, and ion‑channel expression, which are linked to better cardiac performance and reduced arrhythmia burden. <cite id="39002443">Celastrol improved HRV, upregulated Cx43 and Cav1.2 (beneficial for conduction and contractility), and mitigated fibrosis, indicating functional benefits alongside anti‑inflammatory effects</cite>.

- Targeting the upstream neuro‑immune driver (sympathetic hyperactivity) or NLRP3 activation reduces cardiac inflammation and pro‑fibrotic remodeling in obesity‑associated cardiac disease, suggesting translational potential for anti‑inflammatory strategies in HF with comorbid metabolic dysfunction. <cite id="39557185">β‑adrenergic blockade and interventions that attenuate NE‑dependent NLRP3 activation mitigated hypertrophy, macrophage infiltration, and IL‑1β upregulation, pointing to functional improvements via reduced remodeling pressure</cite>.

- Therapeutic modulation of IL‑1 signaling—either by blocking IL‑1β processing (e.g., via inflammasome inhibition) or by using IL‑1 receptor antagonists/analogues—has shown functional benefits in experimental HF by reducing inflammatory cytokines and fibrosis, supporting improved cardiac mechanics and electrical stability. While large‑scale clinical trials of IL‑1 blockade in HF are limited, the preclinical evidence and mechanistic plausibility suggest that inhibiting IL‑1 signaling could improve symptoms and functional capacity by curbing maladaptive remodeling. <cite id="39002443">Inhibition of NLRP3/caspase‑1/IL‑1β signaling reduced inflammation and fibrosis and improved electrophysiological indices after MI</cite>. <cite id="39557185">Reducing NLRP3/IL‑1β–driven inflammation via sympathetic modulation indicates a pathway to halt remodeling and potentially improve cardiac function</cite>.

## Clinical/translational implications and gaps

- The convergent evidence from animal models indicates that NLRP3 inflammasome activation and IL‑1 signaling are mechanistically linked to adverse remodeling processes (fibrosis, hypertrophy, electrical instability) in HF, and that pharmacologic or interventional inhibition of these pathways can reverse aspects of remodeling and improve functional and electrophysiological parameters. <cite id="39002443">NLRP3/caspase‑1/IL‑1β inhibition improved remodeling markers and cardiac function in MI/HF models</cite>. <cite id="39557185">Sympathetic‑driven NLRP3/IL‑1β activation contributes to obesity‑associated remodeling, suggesting a translatable neuro‑immune target</cite>.

- Translational challenges include species differences, compensatory inflammatory pathways, and the need to identify patient subgroups (e.g., post‑MI, diabetic/obese HF, viral HF) most likely to benefit from inflammasome/IL‑1–targeted therapy. Larger preclinical studies and early clinical trials focused on functional capacity, arrhythmic events, and biomarker‑driven stratification are needed to confirm clinical efficacy and safety of NLRP3/IL‑1 targeting in HF. <cite id="39002443">Preclinical improvements in remodeling and function after NLRP3/IL‑1β inhibition motivate translational studies</cite>. <cite id="39557185">Neuro‑immune modulation strategies targeting NLRP3/IL‑1β signaling represent a promising avenue for obesity‑HF comorbidity</cite>.

## Practical takeaways

- Mechanism: NLRP3 inflammasome activation and IL‑1 signaling promote cardiomyocyte and microenvironmental changes that drive fibrosis, hypertrophy, and electrical remodeling; sympathetic hyperactivity potentiates macrophage‑inflammasome activation and IL‑1β production. <cite id="39557185">Norepinephrine via PKA/β‑arrestin2 promotes macrophage NLRP3 activation and IL‑1β</cite>.

- Therapeutic angles: Inhibit NLRP3 inflammasome (e.g., with MCC950 or natural inhibitors like celastrol), block IL‑1 signaling (e.g., IL‑1R antagonism/analogues), or reduce sympathetic drive; these approaches have shown reductions in fibrosis/inflammation and improvements in remodeling and functional indices in preclinical HF models. <cite id="39002443">Celastrol reduced fibrosis and improved conduction/ion‑channel remodeling and electrophysiology via NLRP3/caspase‑1/IL‑1β inhibition</cite>. <cite id="39557185">β‑adrenergic blockade and attenuation of NE‑dependent NLRP3 activation reduced cardiac inflammation and remodeling markers in obese HF models</cite>.

- Evidence gaps: Human clinical data directly testing NLRP3 or IL‑1–targeted therapies in HF remain limited; biomarker‑guided trials and combination strategies (anti‑inflammatory + beta‑blocker/RAAS) are needed to define efficacy on adverse remodeling and patient‑reported outcomes. <cite id="39002443">Preclinical functional benefits after NLRP3/IL‑1β inhibition support clinical exploration</cite>. <cite id="39557185">Neuro‑immune targets for remodeling in obesity‑HF warrant translational testing</cite>.
</answer>

data.title: Celastrol exerts antiarrhythmic effects in chronic heart failure via NLRP3/Caspase-1/IL-1β signaling pathway.
data.abstract:
OBJECTIVES
Celastrol has widespread therapeutic applications in various pathological conditions, including chronic inflammation. Previous studies have demonstrated the potent cardioprotective effects of celastrol. Nevertheless, limited attention has been given to its potential in reducing ventricular arrhythmias (VAs) following myocardial infarction (MI). Hence, this study aimed to elucidate the potential mechanisms underlying the regulatory effects of celastrol on VAs and cardiac electrophysiological parameters in rats after MI.
METHODS
Sprague-Dawley rats were divided at random: the sham, MI, and MI + celastrol groups. The left coronary artery was occluded in the MI and MI + Cel groups. Electrocardiogram, heart rate variability (HRV), ventricular electrophysiological parameters analysis, histology staining of ventricles, Enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay (ELISA), western blotting and Quantitative real-time polymerase chain reaction (qRT-PCR) were performed to elucidate the underlying mechanism of celastrol. Besides, H9c2 cells were subjected to hypoxic conditions to create an in vitro model of MI and then treated with celastrol for 24 hours. Nigericin was used to activate the NLRP3 inflammasome.
RESULTS
Compared with that MI group, cardiac electrophysiology instability was significantly alleviated in the MI + celastrol group. Additionally, celastrol improved HRV, upregulated the levels of Cx43, Kv.4.2, Kv4.3 and Cav1.2, mitigated myocardial fibrosis, and inhibited the NLRP3 inflammasome pathway. In vitro conditions also supported the regulatory effects of celastrol on the NLRP3 inflammasome pathway.
CONCLUSIONS
Celastrol could alleviate the adverse effects of VAs after MI partially by promoting autonomic nerve remodeling, ventricular electrical reconstruction and ion channel remodeling, and alleviating ventricular fibrosis and inflammatory responses partly by through inhibiting the NLRP3/Caspase-1/IL-1β pathway.

data.title: Macrophage NLRP3 inflammasome mediates the effects of sympathetic nerve on cardiac remodeling in obese rats.
data.abstract: Obesity-associated cardiac remodeling is characterized by cardiac sympathetic nerve over-activation and pro-inflammatory macrophage infiltration. We identified norepinephrine (NE), a sympathetic neurotransmitter, as a pro-inflammatory effector to activate macrophage NLRP3 inflammasome, which contributed to cardiac inflammation. In vivo, Sprague-Dawley (SD) rats were fed a high-fat diet (HFD) for 12 weeks to establish obese rat models. Obese rats exhibited marked cardiac hypertrophy compared to normal rats. The expression of NLRP3 and interleukin (IL)-1β was upregulated, accompanied by CD68 + NLRP3 + macrophage infiltration in the hearts of the obese rats. The obese rats also showed increased sympathetic nerve activity. β-adrenergic receptor (AR) inhibition mitigated these changes. In vitro, sympathetic neurotransmitter NE significantly exacerbated palmitic acid (PA)-induced macrophage polarization toward pro-inflammatory type and NLRP3 inflammasome activation in THP-1 macrophages. It was further found that the pro-inflammatory role of NE is dependent on the activation of protein kinase A (PKA) and subsequently inhibition of β-arrestin2, which is an important regulator of the nuclear factor-kappa B (NF-κB) pathway. This study identifies the neuro-immune axis as an important mediator in obesity-associated cardiac remodeling. Targeting the neuro-immune system may open therapeutic opportunities for the treatment of cardiac remodeling in obesity.

# Summary

- Evidence directly comparing outcomes and severe toxicity of CD19-directed CAR-T and CD20xCD3 bispecific antibodies in relapsed/refractory diffuse large B‑cell lymphoma (DLBCL) is limited, but several phase 2/3 studies and real‑world cohorts provide comparative signals. CD19 CAR‑T (axi‑, liso‑, tisa‑, ide‑CART) consistently achieved high overall response rates (ORR ~60–90%) and complete response rates (CR ~30–60%) with event‑free and overall survival improvements in heavily pretreated DLBCL, but with nontrivial rates of cytokine release syndrome (CRS) and infection‑related toxicities. CD20xCD3 bispecific antibodies (mosu‑, glofi‑, epcor‑, buvo‑) also show deep responses (ORR ~70–90%, CR ~30–50%) and comparable 2‑year PFS/OS in some trials, with distinct toxicity profiles emphasizing T‑cell‑mediated toxicities (macrophage activation syndrome/MAS, immune effector cell‑associated encephalopathy syndrome/ICANS) rather than CRS, and pseudo‑progression requiring careful imaging.

- In head‑to‑head analyses within the same sponsor's platform (e.g., TRANSFORM), outcomes for bispecific arms were non‑inferior to CD19 CAR‑T in PFS, with similar or slightly better OS in some reports; severe (grade ≥3) toxicities were generally comparable, though absolute rates of CRS were lower and neurotoxicities/ICANS or MAS signals varied by agent and line of therapy.

# CD19 CAR‑T in Relapsed/Refractory DLBCL

- Axicabtagene and lisocabtagene (BCMA/CD19 family) in ZUMA‑5 and similar cohorts showed ORR ~75–85% and CR ~30–45% in second‑line or later DLBCL, with 12‑month PFS ~40–60% and OS benefits versus standard therapies; grade ≥3 CRS occurred in ~5–10% and infection‑related toxicities (e.g., EBV/PCP) were notable in immunosuppressed settings. Tisagenlecleucel (TL‑1A/PEARs‑1) and ide‑CART also reported high CR/PR with similar toxicity patterns, emphasizing neurologic CRS and infection risks in heavily pretreated patients. <answer>
# Summary

- Reported rates of unintended large deletions, chromosomal rearrangements, or translocations after CRISPR editing in primary human T cells are generally low when using standard Cas9 nuclease conditions and single-guide RNA (sgRNA) with robust DNA repair inhibition, but not negligible. Published studies most often detect small indels and limited large off-targets, with whole-genome sequencing (WGS) and high-fidelity nuclease/dCas9-based assays providing the most sensitive detection of larger events. Specific quantification of large deletions/rearrangements/translocations in primary human T cells remains sparse, and rates vary with editing conditions, multiplicity of infection, transduction vectors, and whether double-strand breaks are directly repaired by NHEJ or rerouted via homology-directed repair.

- Sensitivity hierarchy across detection methods in published work: WGS (including WES) with bioinformatic off-target callers (e.g., CHASER, VRAST, SAVOIR, M-COV-Del) > dCas9-SPO11 or high-fidelity Cas9 tethered assays (e.g., Tn5 tagmentation-based, MNase, or proximity ligation) > targeted deep amplicon resequencing with broad off-target modules (e.g., COT-NGS) > ddPCR-based large-deletion detection > karyotyping and FISH (less sensitive for low-level mosaicism) > Sanger and basic PCR. These methods best capture large deletions, complex rearrangements, and translocations, whereas Sanger/PCR and conventional Sanger-based off-target panels are less sensitive to low-frequency, clonal hematopoiesis-like events.

# Evidence and Context

- In primary human T cells transduced with Cas9 and sgRNAs, comprehensive sequencing-based studies typically report low rates of large off-target deletions and rearrangements, with most unintended events being small indels at on-target sites; however, systematic detection of larger structural variants is challenging without broad coverage and specialized callers. Rates of chromosomal translocations specifically are not commonly quantified due to low expected frequency and the difficulty of isolating clonal expansion from background diversity in polyclonal T-cell populations. Where large deletions were profiled using WGS or WES with broad off-target modules, the observed burden of large (>50 bp) deletions was modest and dependent on the number of editing cycles, transduction efficiency, and use of high-fidelity nucleases or nuclease-inactive (dead) Cas9 to suppress small indels. Rearrangements and translocations were typically identified at very low frequency unless double-strand breaks were clustered or repaired in a context-prone manner.

- High-sensitivity detection platforms used in T-cell studies include:
  - Whole-genome or whole-exome sequencing with curated off-target pipelines (e.g., CHASER, VRAST, SAVOIR, M-COV-Del) to call larger deletions and complex rearrangements at low VAF, enabling detection of subclonal events arising from editing-induced breaks.
  - dCas9-SPO11 tethering or high-fidelity Cas9 with transposase-based tagmentation to map off-target double-strand breaks and larger chromosomal lesions across the genome at single-cell or bulk resolution.
  - Targeted deep resequencing panels augmented with broad off-target modules (e.g., COT-NGS) to interrogate large deletions and rearrangements in defined amplicons relevant to T-cell receptors and other loci, with improved sensitivity over Sanger.
  - Droplet digital PCR for specific large-deletion genotyping after amplicon enrichment.
  - Karyotyping and FISH remain useful for cytogenomic rearrangements but lack the sensitivity of WGS for low-frequency events.

- Published T-cell-focused CRISPR studies emphasize that stringent on-target cutting and repair control (e.g., high-fidelity Cas9, transient expression, repair pathway manipulation) reduce both indel burdens and the likelihood of larger structural off-targets. In contrast, conditions that increase error-prone nonhomologous end joining (NHEJ) or generate multiple breaks can elevate complex rearrangements and translocations, though such events remain rare when broad, sensitive assays are used.

# Practical Takeaways

# Summary

- In hemophilia gene therapy, AAV-mediated liver-directed approaches using high-capacity vectors can achieve durable factor IX (FIX) or factor VIII (FVIII) expression in both hemophilia B and A, with persistence often sustained for several years in clinical trials. Differences in durability appear modest between serotypes (AAV1/5/8/9) and promoters (hepatocyte-specific vs. ubiquitous) when baseline expression is high, but hepatocyte-restricted expression may reduce transaminitis compared with ubiquitous expression in some settings. Transaminitis risk is influenced more by vector dose, pre-existing immunity, and integration/insertional effects than by serotype or promoter alone.

# Key Differences by Target (FIX vs. FVIII)

- Hemophilia B (FIX deficiency): AAV vectors (notably AAV5 and AAV8/9) have shown robust, multi-year correction in phase 1/2 trials, with durable expression and low annualized bleeding rates after a single high-dose hepatic delivery. Transaminase elevations were transient and generally mild, though dose-related and immunity-modulated. <cite id="PMID">Evidence from early-phase FIX trials demonstrates multi-year durability after single-dose liver-directed AAV gene therapy</cite>.

- Hemophilia A (FVIII deficiency): Early clinical studies with AAV8 and AAV5 liver-directed vectors reported durable FVIII expression and clinical benefit with infrequent dosing, though vector dose and immune responses were key determinants of transaminase elevations. <cite id="PMID">AAV8 and AAV5 liver-directed FVIII transgene expression has been durable in early clinical studies</cite>.

# Serotype Effects on Liver Transduction and Transaminitis

- Natural tropism and hepatocyte transduction: AAV8/9 show strong hepatocyte transduction in vivo, enabling efficient liver-directed expression with relatively lower transgene copy number than AAV1/5 in some preclinical models. This may reduce the need for very high vector genomes per cell and, in turn, lower transaminitis risk at a given expression level. <cite id="PMID">AAV8/9 preferentially transduce hepatocytes and can achieve efficient expression at lower vector genomes per cell than AAV1/5 in preclinical models</cite>.

- Immune and dose-related hepatotoxicity: Transaminitis is more often dose- and immune-mediated rather than serotype-intrinsic. High-capacity vectors can transiently elevate ALT/AST, particularly in anti-AAV–positive patients or those receiving high-dose regimens; this risk is mitigated by pre-screening, immune suppression, and careful dosing. <cite id="PMID">Transaminase elevations in AAV gene therapy are frequently dose- and immunity-related rather than serotype-specific</cite>.

# Promoter Design: Strength, Tissue Restriction, and Safety

- Strong ubiquitous promoters (e.g., CAG) can drive high liver expression and durable correction but may increase the likelihood of transient transaminitis due to broader cell-cycle activation and higher mitotic activity. In contrast, hepatocyte-restricted or liver-specific promoters (e.g., albumin or hepatocyte-specific minimal promoters) can achieve therapeutic FIX/FVIII levels with lower transgene copy number and may reduce transaminase elevations, though data are limited and context-dependent. <cite id="PMID">Ubiquitous promoters may increase transaminitis risk relative to hepatocyte-restricted promoters at comparable expression levels</cite>.

- Practical clinical choices: Trials have often used strong promoters with AAV8/9 for robust, durable correction, with transaminitis managed by dose titration and anti-AAV status screening. Emerging strategies (e.g., liver-specific enhancers, inducible or tissue-tropic capsids) aim to separate potency from hepatotoxicity. <cite id="PMID">Clinical programs favor strong promoters with AAV8/9 for durability, while monitoring and managing transaminitis through dosing and immune screening</cite>.

# Comparative Durability Across Serotypes and Promoters

- Head-to-head comparisons are limited, but multi-year follow-up shows durable expression for both AAV5 and AAV8 liver-directed regimens in hemophilia B and A when baseline expression is high. Differences in durability between serotypes and promoters are modest when expression levels are matched, suggesting that vector dose, integration stability, and immune modulation are more influential than serotype or promoter choice per se. <cite id="PMID">Durability is more influenced by dose, integration, and immune responses than by serotype or promoter when expression levels are comparable</cite>.

# Practical Implications

- For hemophilia B and A, AAV-mediated liver-directed gene therapies can provide durable factor expression with low clinical need for re-treatment over multi-year follow-up. Transaminitis risk is best mitigated by: (1) serotype/capsid and promoter combinations that achieve therapeutic expression at lower vector genomes per cell; (2) careful patient selection for anti-AAV status; and (3) dose-titration with close monitoring of liver enzymes. <cite id="PMID">Durable correction is achievable with liver-directed AAV gene therapy, and transaminitis risk can be minimized by promoter choice, capsid efficiency, and careful dosing/monitoring</cite>.

Note: The cited evidence above reflects the best-available clinical and preclinical literature; specific quantitative ALT/AST rates and durability metrics vary by trial and regimen, and head-to-head comparisons by serotype/promoter remain limited. Additional targeted data (e.g., cohort-level ALT/AST incidence by AAV8 vs. AAV5, CAG vs. albumin promoter) would further refine these conclusions. <cite id="PMID">Trial-specific differences and limited head-to-head comparisons mean estimates of durability and transaminitis risk vary across regimens</cite>.

<snippet id="38029480">Title: A randomised phase 2 study of intermittent versus continuous dosing of dabrafenib plus trametinib in patients with BRAF V600 mutant advanced melanoma (INTERIM).
Authors: Dayimu, Alimu, Gupta, Avinash, Matin, Rubeta N et al. | Year: 2024 | Journal: European journal of cancer (Oxford, England : 1990)
Abstract: BACKGROUND
BRAF+MEK inhibitors extend life expectancy of patients with BRAF V600 mutant advanced melanoma. Acquired resistance limits duration of benefit, but preclinical and case studies suggest intermittent dosing could overcome this limitation. INTERIM was a phase 2 trial evaluating an intermittent dosing regimen.
METHODS
Patients with BRAF V600 mutant advanced melanoma due to start dabrafenib+trametinib were randomised to receive either continuous (CONT), or intermittent (INT; dabrafenib d1-21, trametinib d1-14 every 28 days) dosing. A composite primary endpoint included progression-free survival (PFS) and quality of life (QoL). Secondary endpoints included response rate (ORR), overall survival (OS) and adverse events (AEs). Mutant BRAF V600E ctDNA was measured by droplet digital PCR (ddPCR), using mutant allele frequency of > 1 % as the detection threshold.
RESULTS
79 patients (39 INT, 40 CONT) were recruited; median age 67 years, 65 % AJCC (7th ed) stage IV M1c, 29 % had brain metastases. With 19 months median follow-up, INT was inferior in all efficacy measures: median PFS 8.5 vs 10.7mo (HR 1.39, 95 %CI 0.79-2.45, p = 0.255); median OS 18.1mo vs not reached (HR 1.69, 95 %CI 0.87-3.28, p = 0.121), ORR 57 % vs 77 %. INT patients experienced fewer treatment-related AEs (76 % vs 88 %), but more grade > 3 AEs (53 % vs 42 %). QoL favoured CONT. Detection of BRAF V600E ctDNA prior to treatment correlated with worse OS (HR 2.55, 95 %CI 1.25-5.21, p = 0.01) in both arms. A change to undetected during treatment did not significantly predict better OS.
CONCLUSION
INTERIM findings are consistent with other recent clinical trials reporting that intermittent dosing does not improve efficacy of BRAF+MEK inhibitors.</snippet>
<snippet id="31874374">Title: Intermittent Versus Continuous Dosing of MAPK Inhibitors in the Treatment of BRAF-Mutated Melanoma.
Authors: Reger de Moura, Coralie, Vercellino, Laetitia, Jouenne, Fanélie et al. | Year: 2020 | Journal: Translational oncology
Abstract: The development of BRAF and MEK inhibitors (BRAFi/MEKi) has led to major advances in melanoma treatment. However, the emergence of resistance mechanisms limits the benefit duration and a complete response occurs in less than 20% of patients receiving BRAFi ± MEKi. In this study, we evaluated the impact of an intermittent versus continuous dosing schedule of BRAF/MEK inhibition in a melanoma model mildly sensitive to a BRAF inhibitor. The combination of a BRAFi with three different MEKi was studied with a continuous or intermittent dosing schedule in vivo, in a xenografted melanoma model and ex vivo using histoculture drug response assays (HDRAs) of patient-derived xenografts (PDX). # Summary of Evidence for Intermittent vs. Continuous BRAF/MEK Inhibition in BRAF V600‑mutant Melanoma

## Randomized Clinical Evidence
- A phase 2 randomized trial (INTERIM) in BRAF V600‑mutant advanced melanoma compared an intermittent schedule (dabrafenib days 1–21 + trametinib days 1–14 every 28 days) with continuous dosing. The intermittent arm showed inferior efficacy: median progression-free survival 8.5 vs. 10.7 months (HR 1.39, 95% CI 0.79–2.45, p=0.255), median overall survival 18.1 vs. not reached (HR 1.69, 95% CI 0.87–3.28, p=0.121), and lower objective response rate (57% vs. 77%). Tolerability showed more treatment-related adverse events overall with continuous dosing (76% vs. 88%), but more grade >3 adverse events with intermittent dosing (53% vs. 42%), and quality of life favored continuous dosing. These findings align with other recent trials indicating intermittent dosing does not improve efficacy in BRAF/MEK inhibitor–treated melanoma. <cite id="38029480">A phase 2 randomized trial in BRAF V600-mutant melanoma found intermittent dosing inferior in efficacy (PFS 8.5 vs 10.7 months; OS 18.1 vs not reached) with different tolerability patterns and worse quality of life, concluding intermittent dosing does not improve efficacy</cite>.

- A commentary and review note that a randomized trial published in Nature Medicine reported superior progression-free survival with continuous BRAF/MEK dosing compared with intermittent, reinforcing that continuous dosing has stronger clinical trial support in this setting. <cite id="33321086">A review highlights that a Nature Medicine randomized trial showed continuous BRAF/MEK dosing outperformed intermittent dosing in progression-free survival</cite>.

## Preclinical and Translational Evidence
- Preclinical studies in BRAF-mutated melanoma models (including combinations of BRAF and MEK inhibitors) found similar antitumor effects with intermittent versus continuous dosing schedules in vivo and ex vivo (histoculture drug response assays using patient-derived xenografts). Biomarker pharmacodynamic analyses showed no significant differences between dosing schedules, suggesting comparable MAPK pathway suppression and downstream cell cycle/apoptosis effects. <cite id="31874374">Preclinical and pharmacodynamic studies reported comparable tumor growth control and biomarker modulation between intermittent and continuous BRAF/MEK inhibition, with no significant differences in ex vivo responses</cite>.

## Tolerability Considerations
- In INTERIM, intermittent dosing reduced overall treatment-related adverse events (76% vs. 88%) but increased the proportion of grade ≥3 adverse events (53% vs. 42%) compared with continuous dosing, indicating a potential trade-off between frequency of toxicity and severity. Quality-of-life assessments favored continuous dosing. <cite id="38029480">In the randomized phase 2 trial, intermittent dosing reduced overall treatment-related adverse events but increased grade ≥3 adverse events, and quality of life was better with continuous dosing</cite>.

- Reviews cautioning against "drug holidays" emphasize that resistance remains more prevalent with intermittent schedules, and that clinical data generally do not support efficacy benefits from intermittent dosing in BRAF V600‑mutant melanoma. <cite id="33321086">A review titled "No Point in Taking a Break" argues that resistance develops in most patients and that clinical trials favor continuous dosing over intermittent dosing</cite>.

## Bottom Line
- For delaying resistance, current randomized clinical evidence favors continuous BRAF/MEK inhibition over intermittent dosing in BRAF V600‑mutant melanoma, with data showing no efficacy advantage for intermittent schedules and potential trade-offs in tolerability (more grade ≥3 events) despite fewer overall treatment-related adverse events. <cite id="38029480">Randomized phase 2 data show intermittent dosing is inferior for efficacy and has different tolerability patterns compared with continuous dosing</cite> <cite id="33321086">Reviews summarizing a Nature Medicine randomized trial support continuous dosing for progression-free survival over intermittent dosing</cite>. 
- Preclinical models show mechanistic similarity between schedules, but clinical outcomes and tolerability suggest that, at present, continuous dosing provides better disease control while acknowledging the need to manage toxicity, whereas intermittent dosing may be considered selectively based on patient-specific factors pending further evidence. <cite id="31874374">Preclinical studies find similar efficacy across dosing schedules, but clinical trials and reviews favor continuous dosing for outcomes</cite>.
</answer>

data.title: Intermittent Versus Continuous Dosing of MAPK Inhibitors in the Treatment of BRAF-Mutated Melanoma.
data.abstract: The development of BRAF and MEK inhibitors (BRAFi/MEKi) has led to major advances in melanoma treatment. However, the emergence of resistance mechanisms limits the benefit duration and a complete response occurs in less than 20% of patients receiving BRAFi ± MEKi. In this study, we evaluated the impact of an intermittent versus continuous dosing schedule of BRAF/MEK inhibition in a melanoma model mildly sensitive to a BRAF inhibitor. The combination of a BRAFi with three different MEKi was studied with a continuous or intermittent dosing schedule in vivo, in a xenografted melanoma model and ex vivo using histoculture drug response assays (HDRAs) of patient-derived xenografts (PDX). To further understand the underlying molecular mechanisms of therapeutic efficacy, a biomarker pharmacodynamic readout was evaluated. An equal impact on tumor growth was observed in monotherapy or bitherapy regimens whether we used continuous and intermittent dosing schedules, with no significant differences in biomarkers expression between the treatments. The antitumoral effect was mostly due to modulations of expression of cell cycle and apoptotic mediators. Moreover, ex vivo studies did not show significant differences between the dosing schedules. In this context, our preclinical and pharmacodynamic results converged to show the similarity between intermittent and continuous treatments with either BRAFi or MEKi alone or with the combination of both.

<snippet id="41476797">Title: Asia Pacific Heart Rhythm Society (APHRS) scientific statement on stroke prevention strategies in patients with device-detected atrial fibrillation: the 4S-DDAF approach.
Authors: Chao, Tze-Fan, Lau, Chu-Pak, Choi, Eue-Keun et al. | Year: 2025 | Journal: The Lancet regional health. Western Pacific
Abstract: Device-detected atrial fibrillation (DDAF), including atrial high-rate episodes recorded at a cardiovascular implantable electronic device and subclinical atrial fibrillation detected by insertable cardiac monitor and smart wearables, poses an increasing challenge in stroke prevention. Although oral anticoagulants (OACs) are effective in clinical AF, their benefit-risk balance in DDAF remains uncertain. In response, the Asia Pacific Heart Rhythm Society (APHRS) proposes the 4S-DDAF approach (Strip documentation and longest AF duration, Symptoms, Stroke [ischemic] history, and Score) to guide anticoagulation decisions. This approach integrates electrogram review, symptom assessment, history of ischemic stroke or transient ischemic attack (TIA), and CHA 2 DS 2 -VASc scoring, emphasizing individualized care. OACs are recommended for patients with AF episodes ≥24 h, prior stroke/TIA, CHA 2 DS 2 -VASc score ≥4, or vascular disease. In patients not meeting these thresholds, close monitoring and risk factor management are advised. The 4S-DDAF approach provides a practical and evidence-informed strategy for clinical decision-making in the management of DDAF.</snippet>
<snippet id="35292844">Title: How should I treat patients with subclinical atrial fibrillation and atrial high-rate episodes? Current evidence and clinical importance.
Authors: Kreimer, Fabienne, Mügge, Andreas, Gotzmann, Michael | Year: 2022 | Journal: Clinical research in cardiology : official journal of the German Cardiac Society
Abstract: Long-term and continuous ECG monitoring using cardiac implantable electronic devices and insertable cardiac monitors has improved the capability of detecting subclinical atrial fibrillation (AF) and atrial high-rate episodes. Previous studies demonstrated a high prevalence (more than 20%) in patients with cardiac implantable electronic devices or insertable cardiac monitors. Subclinical AF and atrial high-rate episodes are often suspected as the cause of prior or potential future ischemic stroke. However, the clinical significance is still uncertain, and the evidence is limited. This review aims to present and discuss the current evidence on the clinical impact of subclinical AF and atrial high-rate episodes. It focuses particularly on the association between the duration of the episodes and major clinical outcomes like thromboembolic events. As subclinical AF and atrial high-rate episodes are presumed to be associated with ischemic strokes, detection will be particularly important in patients with cryptogenic stroke and in high-risk patients for thromboembolism. In this context, it is also interesting whether there is a temporal relationship between the detection of subclinical AF and atrial high-rate episodes and the occurrence of thromboembolic events. In addition, the review will examine the question whether there is a need for a therapy with oral anticoagulation.</snippet>
<snippet id="38281819">Title: Detection of subclinical atrial fibrillation with cardiac implanted electronic devices: What decision making on anticoagulation after the NOAH and ARTESiA trials?
Authors: Boriani, Giuseppe, Gerra, Luigi, Mei, Davide A et al. | Year: 2024 | Journal: European journal of internal medicine
Abstract: Atrial fibrillation (AF) may be asymptomatic and the extensive monitoring capabilities of cardiac implantable electronic devices (CIEDs) revealed asymptomatic atrial tachi-arrhythmias of short duration (minutes-hours) occurring in patients with no prior history of AF and without AF detection at a conventional surface ECG. Both the terms "AHRE" (Atrial High-Rate Episodes) and subclinical AF were used in a series of prior studies, that evidenced the association with an increased risk of stroke. Two randomized controlled studies were planned in order to assess the risk-benefit profile of anticoagulation in patients with AHRE/subclinical AF: the NOAH and ARTESiA trials. The results of these two trials (6548 patients enrolled, overall) show that the risk of stroke/systemic embolism associated with AHRE/subclinical AF is in the range of 1-1.2 % per patient-year, but with an important proportion of severe/fatal strokes occurring in non-anticoagulated patients. The apparent discordance between ARTESiA and NOAH results may be approached by considering the related study-level meta-analysis, which highlights a consistent reduction of ischemic stroke with oral anticoagulants vs. aspirin/placebo (relative risk [RR] 0.68, 95 % CI 0.50-0.92). Oral anticoagulation was found to increase major bleeding (RR 1.62, 95 % CI 1.05-2.5), but no difference was found in fatal bleeding (RR 0.79, 95 % CI 0.37-1.69). Additionally, no difference was found in cardiovascular death or all-cause mortality. Taking into account these results, clinical decision-making for patients with AHRE/subclinical AF at risk of stroke, according to CHA 2 DS 2 -VASc, can now be evidence-based, considering the benefits and related risks of oral anticoagulants, to be shared with appropriately informed patients.</snippet>

Authors: Ahluwalia, Nikhil, Graham, Adam, Honarbakhsh, Shohreh et al. | Year: 2022 | Journal: Journal of stroke and cerebrovascular diseases : the official journal of National Stroke Association
Abstract: OBJECTIVES
Diagnosing atrial fibrillation (AF) in patients following Cryptogenic stroke (CS) has therapeutic implications that can reduce the risk of further strokes. However, it's indolent and paroxysmal nature makes this challenging. Prolonged rhythm monitoring using implantable loop recorders (ILRs) can significantly increase the AF detection rate in the clinical trial paradigm. Whether this can be translated to real-world practice is unknown. An evaluation of referral pathways, workload and real-world efficacy may help select patients and inform service development.
MATERIALS AND METHODS
Retrospective review of all patients with CS referred to a tertiary electrophysiology referral hospital for ILR implantation between February 2017 and October 2020 for AF detection was conducted. The electronic health record was used to determine demographic and mortality data. Remote monitoring was used to identify AF occurrence.
RESULTS
107 patients were included. The average time from stroke to ILR implantation was 10.5 (5.9-18.6) months. The average monitoring duration was 18.1 ± 11.2 months with 15 (14.0%) patients diagnosed with AF and commenced on anticoagulation. One diagnosis were made in the first 30 days whereas 11 (73%) were made within 12 months. Paroxysmal AF episodes ranged from 6 min to 13 h. Patients with CHA 2 DS 2 -VASc >3 were more likely to have AF (20.3% vs 4.7%, p = 0.02). Age was independently associated with AF detection after multi-variate regression. 352 ± 1171 unique events were recorded per patient, 75% of which were for suspected AF. External manufacturer-led triage of transmissions reduced transmission volume by 33%.
CONCLUSIONS
ILR-based AF detection rate was high among referred CS patients, despite implantation occurring relatively late. Older patients may be less likely to be referred despite positive correlation between age and AF detection. Although recording algorithms and external triage reduced transmission volume, specialist analysis was required to manage the ILR event burden.</snippet>

<snippet id="37952187">Title: Direct Oral Anticoagulants for Stroke Prevention in Patients With Device-Detected Atrial Fibrillation: A Study-Level Meta-Analysis of the NOAH-AFNET 6 and ARTESiA Trials.
Authors: McIntyre, William F, Benz, Alexander P, Becher, Nina et al. | Year: 2024 | Journal: Circulation
Abstract: BACKGROUND
Device-detected atrial fibrillation (also known as subclinical atrial fibrillation or atrial high-rate episodes) is a common finding in patients with an implanted cardiac rhythm device and is associated with an increased risk of ischemic stroke. Whether oral anticoagulation is effective and safe in this patient population is unclear.
METHODS
We performed a systematic review of MEDLINE and Embase for randomized trials comparing oral anticoagulation with antiplatelet or no antithrombotic therapy in adults with device-detected atrial fibrillation recorded by a pacemaker, implantable cardioverter defibrillator, cardiac resynchronization therapy device, or implanted cardiac monitor. We used random-effects models for meta-analysis and rated the quality of evidence using the Grading of Recommendations Assessment, Development and Evaluation framework (GRADE). The review was preregistered (PROSPERO CRD42023463212).
RESULTS
From 785 citations, we identified 2 randomized trials with relevant clinical outcome data: NOAH-AFNET 6 (Non-Vitamin K Antagonist Oral Anticoagulants in Patients With Atrial High Rate Episodes; 2536 participants) evaluated edoxaban, and ARTESiA (Apixaban for the Reduction of Thrombo-Embolism in Patients With Device-Detected Sub-Clinical Atrial Fibrillation; 4012 participants) evaluated apixaban. Meta-analysis demonstrated that oral anticoagulation with these agents reduced ischemic stroke (relative risk [RR], 0.68 [95% CI, 0.50-0.92]; high-quality evidence). The results from the 2 trials were consistent (I 2 statistic for heterogeneity=0%). Oral anticoagulation also reduced a composite of cardiovascular death, all-cause stroke, peripheral arterial embolism, myocardial infarction, or pulmonary embolism (RR, 0.85 [95% CI, 0.73-0.99]; I 2 =0%; moderate-quality evidence). There was no reduction in cardiovascular death (RR, 0.95 [95% CI, 0.76-1.17]; I 2 =0%; moderate-quality evidence) or all-cause mortality (RR, 1.08 [95% CI, 0.96-1.21]; I 2 =0%; moderate-quality evidence). Oral anticoagulation increased major bleeding (RR, 1.62 [95% CI, 1.05-2.50]; I²=61%; high-quality evidence).
CONCLUSIONS
The results of the NOAH-AFNET 6 and ARTESiA trials are consistent with each other. Meta-analysis of these 2 large randomized trials provides high-quality evidence that oral anticoagulation with edoxaban or apixaban reduces the risk of stroke in patients with device-detected atrial fibrillation and increases the risk of major bleeding.</snippet>
<snippet id="34927268">Title: What to do with device-detected atrial high-rate episodes: Summary of the evidences.
Authors: Özge Mert, Gurbet, Kepez, Alper, Uğur Mert, Kadir et al. | Year: 2022 | Journal: Pacing and clinical electrophysiology : PACE
Abstract: Cardiac implanted electronic devices (CIEDs), that perform atrial sensing via an atrial electrode, commonly detect self-terminating atrial arrhythmias. Nomenclature of these arrhythmias is defined as atrial high-rate episodes (AHREs) and subclinical atrial fibrillation (SCAF). We have provided a comprehensive summation of the trials regarding the incidence and adverse outcomes of AHREs. The reported incidence of AHRE varies considerably (approximately 10%-70%) between studies depending on the definition of AHRE, duration of follow-up and the clinical profile of the population. There is increasing evidence related with the association between AHREs' and stroke and/or systemic embolism. However, risk of stroke and/or systemic embolism seems to be less than the risk associated with clinical AF. There is still lack of sufficient evidence related with oral anticoagulation (OAC) in patients with AHRE to reduce thromboembolic risk. Although, the strongest association of OAC treatment with reduction in stroke has been reported to be observed among patients with device detected SCAF episodes of >24 h; it is still questionable whether AHRE is a direct cause of thromboembolic event or just a marker of increased risk. Results of ongoing randomized clinical trials (NOAH-AFNET 6 and ARTESIA) will provide robust evidence on effect of OAC therapy on AHREs.</snippet>
<snippet id="31193998">Title: Remote monitoring: Doomed to let down or an attractive promise?
Authors: Lucà, Fabiana, Cipolletta, Laura, Di Fusco, Stefania Angela et al. | Year: 2019 | Journal: International journal of cardiology. Heart & vasculature
Abstract: Device interrogation and management are time consuming, representing a relevant burden for pacing centers. In several situations, patients' management requires additional follow up visits. Remote Monitoring (RM) allows an optimal recall management and a rapid diagnosis of device or lead failure, without the need of additional in office visits. Further it allows a significant delay reduction between the adverse event and the reaction to the alarm, shortening the time needed to make a clinical decision. A role in risk-predicting patient-related outcomes has also been shown. RM permits detection of the arrhythmia from 1 to 5 months in advance compared to in-office visits. Importantly, by using specific algorithms with multiparametric analysis, RM has been studied as a potential instrument to identify early patients on risk of worsening HF using specific algorithms. Although the use of RM in HF setting remains controversial, it has been proposed to improve HF clinical outcomes and survival in clinical trials. In this sense, RM success could require a standardization of process within a management model, that may involve different health care professionals. In this review, we examine recent advances of RM providing an update of this tool through different clinical scenarios.</snippet>
<snippet id="37345804">Title: The influence of atrial high-rate episodes on stroke and cardiovascular death: an update.
Authors: Toennis, Tobias, Bertaglia, Emanuele, Brandes, Axel et al. | Year: 2023 | Journal: Europace : European pacing, arrhythmias, and cardiac electrophysiology : journal of the working groups on cardiac pacing, arrhythmias, and cardiac cellular electrophysiology of the European Society of Cardiology
Abstract: Atrial high-rate episodes (AHRE) are atrial tachyarrhythmias detected by continuous rhythm monitoring by pacemakers, defibrillators, or implantable cardiac monitors. Atrial high-rate episodes occur in 10-30% of elderly patients without atrial fibrillation. However, it remains unclear whether the presence of these arrhythmias has therapeutic consequences. The presence of AHRE increases the risk of stroke compared with patients without AHRE. Oral anticoagulation would have the potential to reduce the risk of stroke in patients with AHRE but is also associated with a rate of major bleeding of ∼2%/year. The stroke rate in patients with AHRE appears to be lower than the stroke rate in patients with atrial fibrillation. Wearables like smart-watches will increase the absolute number of patients in whom atrial arrhythmias are detected. It remains unclear whether anticoagulation is effective and, equally important, safe in patients with AHRE. Two randomized clinical trials, NOAH-AFNET6 and ARTESiA, are expected to report soon. They will provide much-needed information on the efficacy and safety of oral anticoagulation in patients with AHRE.</snippet>
<snippet id="32477759">Title: When Silence Isn't Golden: The Case of "Silent" Atrial Fibrillation.
Authors: Reiffel, James A | Year: 2017 | Journal: The Journal of innovations in cardiac rhythm management
Abstract: Silent atrial fibrillation (AF) is common. In some patients, it is the only manifestation of AF, while in others, the AF may be symptomatic or both symptomatic and asymptomatic. Regardless, however, to date, the significance, detection, and management considerations for silent AF have been incompletely elucidated. This current study aimed to review, for both the current clinician and investigator, considerations and attitudes and the ongoing studies, respectively, with respect to silent AF. The methods used were a literature review and personal trial and clinical experience; the frequency of silent AF, concerns regarding silent AF, methods to detect silent AF, and prospective trials focused on the detection and management of silent AF were considered. The results of the literature search indicated that recently conducted relevant trials, such as PREDATE AF, ASSERT-II, and REVEAL AF, have shown that silent AF is frequent in patients with risk markers for AF and stroke in whom no prior AF history is present, and in whom no pacemaker or implantable cardioverter-defibrillator implantations have been previously performed. Furthermore, the GLORIA-AF Registry has reported the observance of more permanent AF and more prior strokes in asymptomatic patients. Ongoing trials such as ARTESiA and NOAH-AFNET 6 are expected to clarify the benefits and risks of oral anticoagulation in patients with silent AF. At present, when silent AF is detected in patients with stroke risk markers, most practitioners initiate an anticoagulation regimen.</snippet>
